response.answer: For robust, policy-relevant findings, use FDR control methods like Benjamini-Hochberg and hierarchical testing for interpretability. E-values and VanderWeele bounds offer additional sensitivity thresholds.

results.title: Practical Multiple Testing Correction in ML
results.content: # Practical Multiple Testing Correction in ML. This blog article provides a comprehensive guide to practical multiple testing corrections in ML. Integrating multiple testing corrections into an ML pipeline involves:. graph TD A["Data Collection"] --> B["Feature Extraction"] B --> C["Exploratory Data Analysis"] C --> D["Multiple Hypothesis Testing"] D --> E["Apply Correction Methods"] E --> F["Model Training & Validation"] F --> G["Result Interpretation"] %% Mathematical check inside diagram subgraph MathChecks [Statistical Considerations] H["Check: $$ \sum_{i=1}^m p_i \leq m \times \alpha $$"] end D --> H. When choosing between multiple testing correction methods, consider:. ### scikit-learn Integration While scikit-learn does not offer a dedicated function for multiple testing corrections, its robust pipeline capabilities allow for integration of custom p-value correction steps in the model training process. A simplified Python snippet: ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd import as mt from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split (42) data_size = 100 X = (data_size, 10) y = (0, 2, data_size) p_values = [] for i in range(X.shape[1]): # Here you would normally conduct a statistical test per feature # For illustration, we simulate p-values p_values.append(()) _, pvals_corrected, _, _ = mt.multipletests(p_values, alpha=0.05, method='fdr_bh') print("Original p-values:", p_values) print("FDR corrected p-values:", pvals_corrected) selected_features = [i for i, p in enumerate(pvals_corrected) if p < 0.05] X_selected = X[:, selected_features] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_selected, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42) model = LogisticRegression() model.fit(X_train, y_train) print("Model accuracy:", model.score(X_test, y_test)) This code integrates multiple testing correction into the pre-modeling phase to select significant features before training a logistic regression model. requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager") BiocManager::install("multtest") library(multtest) result <- mt.rawp2adjp(p_values, proc = "BH") print(result$adjp) ### Practical Examples In R, users often integrate multiple testing correction within broader statistical package workflows. --- ## Conclusion & Next Steps Multiple testing corrections are a fundamental aspect of robust ML workflows—ensuring that statistical inferences drawn from multiple comparisons are reliable and accurate. This article has provided an in-depth exploration of multiple testing methods, from the classical Bonferroni approach to more nuanced FDR control techniques. ### Key Takeaways - Multiple testing increases the risk of false positives, which can be mitigated by carefully selecting and applying correction methods.

results.title: Beyond Bonferroni: Hierarchical Multiple Testing in Empirical Research | NBER
results.content: # Beyond Bonferroni: Hierarchical Multiple Testing in Empirical Research. This paper offers a general, practical review of methods for dealing with multiple hypothesis testing, aimed at applied researchers who must draw inference on multiple outcomes, subgroups, or model specifications but often lack clear guidance on how to proceed. Beyond standard corrections such as Bonferroni, Holm, and false discovery rate controls, we emphasize the value of hierarchical procedures that exploit causal or logical structure to deliver more powerful and interpretable results. Title: Multiple testing correction methods: FDR, q-values vs p-values - biostatsquid.com
# Multiple testing correction methods: FDR, q-values vs p-values. Even if we use a p-value threshold lower than 0.05 (**p-val < 0.05**), this means there is a **5% chance of false positive** – and that is exactly what happened. We might choose a **p value threshold of 0.05.** This means that the probability of saying that a gene is significant when it actually is not, is 5%. With the **Bonferroni correction**, we use a **p-value threshold** of 0.05/1000, so **0.00005.** There is 0.005% chance that we are wrong and the gene is actually not associated with being a morning person. After choosing the appropriate statistical test, we get a p-value for each object, indicating how statistically significant is there association to the beach. If we set a p value threshold of 0.05, it means 15 objects were significantly linked with the beach, and 5 of them were not. Our p-value threshold is 0.05, meaning there is still a 5% probability that we classify an object as being correlated with going to the beach, when actually it is not, **just by chance.**. If we use our first method to correct for multiple testing, the **Bonferroni correction,** we would have to use a p value of 0.00205. False positives, for example, are genes that are not statistically significant, so they are not interesting for us, but just by chance they got a p-value lower than 0.05. In both cases, we get a new list of corrected or **adjusted p-values** for each test. A p-value of 0.05 means that 5% of all tests will result in false positives. So in this case, if we go with objects with a **p-adjusted** or **q-value threshold** of 0.05, it means we are willing to accept 0.75 (so less than 1 object) that’s classified as a beach object when it is not. For example, if you are doing a **pilot study or exploratory analysis** on genes correlated with Alzheimer’s, you want to avoid losing potential interesting genes, but you also don’t want a lot of false positives, so you can use q-values for this. Q-values control the False Discovery Rate (FDR) and are computed from p-values:.
